headline: Approved 83-unit housing development at 110 Leigus Road; continued floating-zone text amendment and 124 Church Street gas station permit to November.
summary: The Commission approved an 83-unit multi-family development at 110 Leigus Road, which includes an offer to deed or restrict 11.3 acres for conservation. It continued the Mixed Use floating zone text amendment and the 124 Church Street gas station permit to November. It also approved a site plan for 60 Carpenter Lane and released a bond at 25 Wall Street.
decisions: Approved the minutes of the September 14, 2026 meeting as submitted, unanimously.
Withdrawn: text amendment #504-26 to add cannabis retailer as a Special Permit use in the RF-40 (Route 5) zone.
Continued the site plan for Times Microwave Systems at 358 Hall Avenue to the November 16, 2026 meeting.
Continued the public hearing on the Mixed Use (MU) District floating zone text amendment for KSCGH Partners, LLC to the November meeting, 5-0.
Continued the Special Permit for a gas station and drive-through store at 124 Church Street to the November meeting, 5-0.
Approved the site plan for an 83-unit multi-family residential development at 110 Leigus Road, subject to conditions, 5-0.
Approved the site plan for a light manufacturing facility with three buildings at 60 Carpenter Lane, subject to conditions, 5-0.
Approved release of the bond for McNulty at 25 Wall Street, unanimously.
Approved use of the parade grounds and other listed locations to install bike racks, unanimously.
Noted as approved four administrative approvals: 59 North Elm St., 824 East Center St. Unit A, 1181 Barnes Rd., and 480 North Colony Rd.

October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 1 
 
Wallingford Planning & Zoning Commission 
Regular Meeting 
Wednesday, October 14, 2026 
7:00 p.m. 
Robert F. Parisi Council Chambers – Town Hall 
Town Hall – 45 South Main Street 
MINUTES 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons called the meeting to order at approximately 7:00 p.m.  
 
The Pledge of Allegiance was recited by all. 
Roll Call:  Present:  James Fitzsimmons, Chair; Jeffrey Kohan, Vice Chair; David Leonardo, Secretary; 
James Seichter, Regular Member; J.P. Venoit, Regular Member; Joseph Sanders, Alternate; Richard 
Benham, Alternate; and Kevin Pagini, Town Planner. 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons noted that the following agenda items will not be heard tonight.  
1. PUBLIC HEARING – #504-26 Text Amendment request for Quinnipiac Valley Growth 
Partners to add cannabis retailer as an allowed use by Special Permit in the RF-40 
(Route 5) Zoning District.  Text amendment will alter Sections §1.4; §6.34; and §4.16.C.  
Withdrawn 
5. SITE PLAN – Site Plan/Times Microwave Systems/358 Hall Avenue #224-26 (continued 
to November 16, 2026 meeting) 
 
Consideration of Minutes – September 14, 2026, Regular Meeting 
Commissioner Kohan:  Motion to approve the Minutes of Monday, September 14, 2026, 
Meeting of the Wallingford Planning and Zoning Commission as submitted. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo:  Second 
 Vote: Unanimous to approve . 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons noted that going forward, the Commission will require all evidence and feedback 
to be received one week prior to the meeting.   
 
PUBLIC HEARING 
2. Text Amendment request for KSCGH Partners, LLC to add a new section §4.27 entitled 
“Mixed Use (MU) District” floating zone to the Town of Wallingford Zoning Regulations  
#505-26 (continuation) 
Commissioner Leonardo noted the additional correspondence. Email from Michele Dellipoali, to Kevin 
Pagini, Town Planner received August 19, 2026; draft text amendment received August 24, 2026; email 
from Dennis Ceneviva, to Kevin Pagini, received September 11, 2026; draft text amendment received 
October 2, 2026 with information on floating zones; Interoffice Memorandum from Thomas Flannery, 
Senior Engineer, Water & Sewer to Kevin Pagini, Town Planner received October 9, 2026; draft text
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 2 
 
amendment received October 9, 2026; Memo from the Department of Engineering, to the Planning & 
Zoning Commission dated October 9. 2026; email from Dennis Ceneviva to Kevin Pagini, Town Planner, 
receive October 14, 2026; letter from Don Crouch, Economic Development Specialist to the Wallingford 
Planning & Zoning Commission, received October 14, 2026; staff comments from Sebastian Velez, 
Environmental and Natural Resources Planner dated October 14, 2026; letter from David Bouvier, 
Fairlawn Farms, dated October 14, 2026; and an Inspection Report from the Wallingford Fire Marshall, 
dated October 14, 2026. 
 
Atty. Dennis Ceneviva, Ceneviva Law Firm, 721 Broad Street, Meriden, and Matt Brutin, Project 
Engineer, BL Companies, presented. 
 
Atty. Ceneviva handed out a copy of his presentation.  The concept of a floating zone was explained at 
the last presentation.  He noted that this is not solely the concept of a property owner, but collaboration 
with the Town.  He explained the floating zone as a district applied to one or more parcels with the 
design goal to provide flexibility balanced by control in the development of land. Flexibility and control 
are given to the Planning & Zoning Commission.  The application to one or more parcels is a legislative 
decision by Planning & Zoning.  This gives broader authority.  He stated that they can’t submit a plan for 
a property if it is not zoned for the use they are seeking.  He stated that this is a multi-layered process. 
First, the zoning district is created. He explained the purpose of the zone.  Then the applicability is 
determined, including certain limitations that Town Staff suggested. Some public comments were also 
included.  They propose a minimum of 40 acres.  An overall conceptual site plan is designed and 
developed with no less than 25% of the gross floor area residential and a minimum of 25% non-
residential.  There is broad discretion on the part of the Commission to approve, deny, or adjust the 
plan.  The Commission would look at traffic, access points, and limit applicability to certain zones.  They 
propose only IX, WI, CA, and CB zones.  They listed 13 permitted uses, one of which provides some 
discretion on the part of the Commission.  They included accessory uses such as a drive-thru.  The site 
plan should include a central open space for pedestrians and bike trails.  For building design, they 
included 40,000 sq. ft. for non-residential buildings and the 1st-floor building facade limited to 400 ft in 
length.  The parking plan was developed with the input of Water & Sewer and the Town Engineer to 
include a standard for impervious surface cover.  Open space has to be a minimum of 50%, and interior 
landscaping is required between parking areas.  The minimum landscape buffers are increased to 150 ft. 
between non-residential and residential. A traffic impact analysis is required, and the Commission can 
request a peer review.  Procedural requirements include an informal meeting/workshop with the 
opportunity for staff and the Commission to review the overall conceptual site plan and comment.  Then 
the application applies for the Zoning Map Amendment to apply the Floating Zone, with a public hearing 
and notification to neighbors. This is when the overall conceptual site plan is shared, but the plan is not 
approved at this point.  Once the zone is approved, then the plan will be submitted for Site Plan 
approval.  The final draft of the text amendment addressed all comments received except for those from 
the Environmental Planner received today.  They are willing to incorporate those comments. 
 
Commissioner Seichter noted that the Commission received quite a few documents today. He stated 
that he appreciates all the work put into this proposal.  He asked about the version of the amendment
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 3 
 
received October 9th that has the applicability size at zero. Atty. Ceneviva replied that it should be 40 
acres.  Commissioner Seichter asked how many possible parcels in town could meet this.   He suggested 
changing it to 60 acres.  He asked about the landscape buffer of 150 ft. for commercial and 100 ft. for 
residential. He stated that he would like to see 150 ft. for both.  He stated that the proposal could result 
in a project with 75% retail.   
 
Atty. Ceneviva stated that there was a concern that the development would be heavily residential, so 
they added the minimum.  As for locations, that is based on the Commission’s discretion, and the 
applicant won’t propose something that will fail. The Commission has discretion. He noted that 75% 
commercial would not meet the parking and impervious surface requirements.  The purpose of this is to 
provide flexibility since we don’t know what the future will bring.  
 
Commissioner Seichter stated that making other uses available in these zones is good.  The possibility of 
75% retail is a concern.  He asked about the setback.  Mr. Pagini replied that in the WI zone the frontage 
setback is 100 ft. Commissioner Seichter noted that the front of the building needs to face the road and 
that should be part of the building design.  Regarding the 50% open space, he asked if that was 
discussed with Water & Sewer. Atty. Ceneviva replied yes, and the Town Engineer, too.  As for the 
setback, he stated that they wanted the buildings to be closer to the road without parking in front.  
 
Commissioner Kohan appreciated the chart that was added to the text amendment.  He stated that a 
floating zone fits the requirements to allow this type of development while still giving Planning & Zoning 
control.  He believes the final draft is good. Regarding the permitted uses, he asked about the maximum 
number of units for a multi-family residential development.  Atty. Ceneviva replied that they added 
some 3-bedroom units based on feedback.  They made the density low enough to discourage too many 
units.  Townhouses would also fit.  The design provides some breadth.  Commissioner Kohan referred to 
the Regulatory paragraph, line 2, stating that it doesn’t make sense. He suggested striking the reference 
to overall character as we can’t say that anymore.  He asked about the two-year limit for development 
in number 3.  Mr. Pagini noted that it is typically five years, but because this changes the entire zone, it 
would revert to the original underlying zones.  Commissioner Kohan noted comments received today 
about the height.  Mr. Pagini stated that the WI allows up to 80 ft if there is enough setback.  
Commissioner Kohan stated that he likes the way this is written and that Planning and Zoning still has 
authority. He thinks this is a win-win. 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons stated that the concept of a floating zone is different.  Conceptually, it works. He 
supports the proposal.  He quoted from the letter received today from the EDC that this is ”a 
coordinated approach to development can create opportunities for shared infrastructure, improved 
internal circulation, and more efficient use of the land and parking.” The letter continues, “The EDC 
office believes that a carefully structured mixed-use floating zone could strengthen Wallingford’s 
economic development toolkit by providing greater flexibility for appropriate large-scale projects while 
retaining meaningful planning, infrastructure, traffic and environmental safeguards.” He stated that he 
would like more time to review the materials due to a lot being received just today.
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 4 
 
Mr. Pagini stated that the applicant worked with staff and addressed the bulk of the comments. Staff is 
happy with the proposal. 
 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
Scott Amore, Jenna Road, stated that this is a creative way to address the recommendations of the 
POCD.  He suggested adaptive reuse of post-industrial properties.  He noted that there is no application 
yet.  He asked if the Commission could change the 40 acres.  He also asked if the Commission could 
create its own amendment.  He stated that he is an advocate for housing with walkable communities.   
 
Don Crouch, Economic Development Specialist, stated that the project should start within two years due 
to the amount of time and resources that would be invested before the site plan is presented.   
 
Ken Lloyd, President of Wallingford Community Farmers Group and an environmentalist, asked how 
many undeveloped acres will be used for the mixed development on Rt. 68.  He is concerned about 
developing this land. We need more information.  The public doesn’t know about this. This would turn 
40 or 60 acres of land into condos and apartments.  It won’t be the same town. 
 
Sheryl Hart, North Elm Street, asked if affordable housing is involved. Is it what’s going to be built first or 
the zoning first?  Chairman Fitzsimmons replied that this application is a zoning text amendment, not 
the application at 110 Leigus Road. Planning is done first.  
 
Craig Fishbein, Grieb Road, stated that zoning is important.  He noted that he couldn’t find the current 
version of the amendment and asked that the public be part of the process. He stated that ultimately 
this is spot zoning and that’s not allowed.  He stated that 60 acres may be more appropriate.  Looking at 
the potential parcel, he stated concern with sight lines.  He noted that the existing berms and plantings 
would go away if the setback is 50 ft.  He is not in favor.  There are other ways to go about this.  He is 
afraid for this land. He noted that there would probably be curb cuts added. 
 
Jessica Wysocki, 76 Knollwood, stated that she is concerned with land conservation.  She would like to 
see the town buy more land for conservation of wetlands.  She is concerned that we will lose the woods 
in that area. 
 
Scott Craig, 31 Leigus Road, stated that he would like to see additional buffering.  When the building was 
built for39-31 Leigus, they put in a large berm and four dense rows of conifer trees for year-round 
coverage.  He can’t see the Blue Cross building.  One or two rows of trees won’t block the view. 
 
Carl Fister, 25 Fairlawn Drive, stated that the buffer requirements are important. He asked about light 
spillover standards and a traffic impact analysis. He asked about limits on high-impact uses. He 
suggested limiting high-turnover commercial uses, such as drive-throughs, from being near residential 
communities.
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 5 
 
Joe Solato, 21 Promontory Drive, stated that the draft amendments are a hot mess with all the revisions.  
The public doesn’t really know about this.  All the affected zones should be notified. He suggested that 
they just propose a zone change for the area they want to develop.  He noted that the current 
regulations are for 40 ft. height. We need to look at the current restrictions. They need to present what 
they want to do. 
 
 
Michelle Dellipoali, 10 Trailside Drive, stated that she just found out about this hearing today and would 
like more time to review the materials.  A visual study with architectural elevations is needed.  She 
would like to add a visual impact assessment on the scenic quality of the area. She asked about noise 
and light issues and truck loading.  She referred to Part B – Applicability; this could result in 75% housing 
or 75% commercial.  Those are not the percentages we should be going to.  Regarding Part D for site 
design, Part 5, residential requirements, she suggested including “apartments, townhouses and ranch-
style condos”.  She asked why the height is 50 ft, when it should be capped at 40 ft. In Section 6, Part D, 
the height of berms should be defined, and details provided on the trees, including multiple rows of 
evergreen trees. On the requirements table of lot and building requirements, the maximum building 
height doesn’t state if it’s commercial or residential.  She tried to find properties in the town that might 
be 40 acres and was offered the grand list and told to figure it out herself. She thanked the Planning & 
Zoning Department and the Commission for their efforts. 
 
Atty. Ceneviva stated that if approved, there will be a plan, but they don’t have one yet.  The only plan 
he has seen is developing the site in accordance with the WI zoning for warehouses. This is not spot 
zoning.  The CT Supreme Court has determined that this type of Floating Zones is appropriate. He agreed 
that setbacks and buffer heights are important.  They would like the opportunity to bring a plan to the 
Commission.  The public would be notified.  He stated that he would be happy to meet with neighbors 
when they have a plan.  The text gives the Commission discretion to deny, as well as allowing a broader 
type of development. This concept has been encouraged by the Town.  He stated that he is happy to 
provide any of these documents to the public. 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons thanked the public for their comments and noted that documents are normally 
available in the Zoning Office, not online.  He proposed continuing the application. 
 
Commissioner Seichter stated that the size should be 60 acres, buffers are very important, and a 150 ft. 
setback would be appropriate.  As for building size, he likes the 40 ft. height. He doesn’t like drive-thru 
locations s.  
 
Atty. Ceneviva noted that the Town Engineer suggested the language on the minimum buffer to include 
that the existing buffers be maintained when possible.  
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons noted that since Commissioner Venoit had to leave, Commissioner Sanders will 
be voting in his place.
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 6 
 
Hearing no further public comment, Chairman Fitzsimmons called for a motion to continue the public 
hearing. 
 
Commissioner Kohan: Motion to continue the public hearing for application #502-26 Text 
Amendment request for KSCGH Partners, LLC to the November meeting. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo: Second 
Vote: Kohan – yes; Leonardo – yes; Seichter – yes; Sanders – yes; Chairman Fitzsimmons  –  
yes. 
The continuation is approved. 
 
 
3. Special Permit request for Atlantis Management Group to demolish an existing building 
and construct a gas station with a 4,500± sq. ft. drive-through retail and convenience store 
at 124 Church St., located in the I-40 (Industrial) District.    #407-26 
Commissioner Leonardo read the legal notice and noted the correspondence.  #407-26 – Special Permit 
request for Atlantis Management Group to demolish an existing building and construct a gas station 
with a 4,500± sq. ft. drive-through retail and convenience store at 124 Church St., located in the I-40 
(Industrial) District.  Correspondence included: email from Kevin Pagini, Town Planner to Annette Ellis, 
Juliano Associates dated July 23, 2026; email from Annette Ellis, Juliano Associates to Kevin Pagini, Town 
Planner dated July 23, 2026; letter from Kevin Pagini, Town Planner to Atlantis Management Group, LLC 
dated July 22, 2026; Memo from the Department of Engineering, to the Planning & Zoning Commission 
received July 29, 2026; email from Thomas Flannery, Senior Engineer, Water & Sewer, to Planning & 
Zoning, dated August 4, 2026; Interoffice Memorandum from Thomas Flannery, Senior Engineer, Water 
& Sewer, to Kevin Pagini, Town Planner, received August 4, 2026; letter from Romeo Valentin, Juliano 
Associates, to Kevin Pagini, Town Planner dated August 31, 2026; Operations & Maintenance Plan 
received from Juliano Associates, received September 2, 2026; Memo from the Department of 
Engineering to the Planning & Zoning Commission received September 4, 2026; email from Sebastian 
Velez, Environmental and Natural Resources Planner to Planning & Zoning received September 9, 2026; 
Inspection Report from the Wallingford Fire Marshal received October 14, 2026; and a revised Traffic 
study, received October 14, 2026. 
 
Starke Hipp, PE, Traffic Engineer, LaBella Associates, Romeo Valentin, Project Engineer, Juliano 
Associates, and Emily Rocha, Dunkin Donuts Franchisee, presented.   
 
Mr. Valentin explained that the site is a 2-acre lot with a 3,100 sq. ft. building that will be demolished.  
They propose building a 4,500 sq. ft. building with 1,400 sq. ft. for a Dunkin drive-thru location, and the 
rest will be a convenience store and gas station with 10 pumps.  They will only allow one-way traffic and 
will provide 23 parking spaces.  They will reduce the existing impervious surface by 66 sq. ft., and thus 
no detention system is required. He explained the stormwater management system.  They will provide 
for two exit lanes, one left, one right.  They will tie into the existing sanitary sewer.  He explained the
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 7 
 
sight line analysis and the vehicle turning analysis.  He added that they are not opposed to reducing 
parking and allowing more grass. 
 
Commissioner Kohan stated a concern with traffic and asked what will be sold at the store.  Mr. Hipp 
replied that it will be an Atlantis Fresh Market, which is a higher-end convenience store.  The food 
service component is Dunkin Donuts.  There will be no indoor seating. Commissioner Kohan asked about 
the food available at Dunkin.  Ms. Rocha replied that they will offer sandwiches, baked goods, and 
coffee.  Commissioner Kohan referred to the traffic study, Table 1.  He asked if the data is from 2022.  
Mr. Hipp replied that the data is published by the DOT and the traffic data is generally good for five 
years. They did not do their own count.  Commissioner Kohan suggested different peak time periods.  He 
noted the comment from the Town Engineer that left-turn exits will be difficult.  He noted that there are 
tractor-trailers from United Concrete that occasionally block traffic. He asked how often the gas trucks 
will be delivering.  Mr. Hipp explained how the peak hours were calculated and that he couldn’t answer 
about the gas deliveries.  Commissioner Kohan asked if there is enough room for the truck to turn 
without affecting the opposing lane.  Mr. Valentin replied yes. Commissioner Kohan stated that this will 
work, but it will be difficult.  He suggested reducing the pumps to four.  Mr. Hipp relayed a response 
from the applicant that they expect two gas deliveries per week and that they will be scheduled to arrive 
during non-peak hours.  He noted that the major component of traffic will be pass-by trips.  Only 25% 
are expected to be new trips.  There will not be a significant increase in the volume of traffic.  He 
compared the trip generation to when it was a restaurant. There should be fewer trips generated.  
Commissioner Kohan disagreed because traffic backs up significantly in both directions now.  He 
proposed making the exit right turn only. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo noted that the Duchess restaurant was not a high traffic generator. This will be 
more of a flow going through the property.  He likes the right-turn-only exit.  He likes the idea but is 
concerned with safety and traffic backing up.  Mr. Hipp noted that customers can self-select and not 
enter if the pumps are full. There will be good visibility from the road.  Commissioner Leonardo asked if 
queuing was studied.  Mr. Hipp replied that he has never done a queuing study for gas pumps.  The 
drive-thru locations provide active capacity.  He understands the safety concerns.   
 
Commissioner Sanders agreed with the concerns on traffic. He noted that there are several other Dunkin 
and 7 Brew locations in the area.  He finds it hard to believe that the traffic study shows less traffic than 
Duchess. He stated that it looks like the fuel truck will clip the building as it drives around.  Mr. Valentin 
replied that they can’t move the driveway further due to the parking. They are using a mountable curb.  
Commissioner Sanders asked if a stuck vehicle or an emergency could end up trapping cars.  Mr. 
Valentin replied that emergency vehicles can drive around the front if necessary. 
 
Commissioner Seichter stated that the site is challenging due to traffic.  He agreed that the peak traffic 
times are different than what’s in the report.  He stated that other drive-thru locations have created 
traffic problems.
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 8 
 
Commissioner Benham asked if this Dunkin franchise has partnered with Atlantis before. Ms. Rocha 
replied that they did partner briefly once for a different format before, but they have partnered with 
other franchisees in the State.  One of their properties has a similar layout.  This concept works well.  
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons asked if the applicant can control the fuel deliveries, including how they enter 
the property to avoid crossing Rt. 68. Mr. Hipp relayed the response from the owner that yes, they 
control the deliveries, including where they come from.  Chairman Fitzsimmons asked about the height 
of the canopy and whether it can handle landscape trucks and vans.  Mr. Hipp replied that there will be 
a 14 ft clearance, which is the state-mandated clearance.  Chairman Fitzsimmons noted the approval 
from 2024 and asked if they have been in contact with the Chief of Police.  Mr. Hipp replied that they 
met with the Police at the initial meeting with staff.  Chairman Fitzsimmons noted that in 2024 it was 
determined that Dunkin customer traffic would be redistributed among Dunkin locations. Ms. Rocha 
agreed.  
 
Manuel Rocha, franchisee for Dunkin Donuts in Wallingford, stated that he has been in business for 30+ 
years.  He wants to do this right. He understands the concerns. They have spent a tremendous amount 
of money on their drive-through locations. They have eliminated cars backing up on Rt. 5. He stated that 
Atlantis is a professional company.  They have two other locations in Wallingford. He doesn’t think this 
will add to the traffic any more than anything else that might go there. 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons referred to the Engineering memo, which states that left turns will require a 
courtesy pullout during peak hours. The left turns will be a challenge.  He asked if they would consider 
restricting it to right turns only. Mr. Hipp offered to do a Gap Analysis. This would involve observing gaps 
between vehicles.  This might provide some clarity. He can also refresh the traffic data.   
 
Mr. Pagini asked the Commission if they want the gap analysis and comments from the Police Chief.  
 
PUBLIC COMMENT 
Craig Fishbein, Grieb Road, stated that he would use this Dunkin location.  He noted that the traffic 
study is murky.  He is concerned with the sight line westerly, down the hill after the overpass.  This will 
slow traffic as people slow to turn in.  Do they really expect to need 10 pumps?  He stated that a right-
turn-only exit will not be popular as there is no easy place to do a U-turn. 
 
Susan Gomes, Edgewood Drive, echoed the heavy traffic and safety concerns. 
 
Frederick Rizzo, Highland Avenue, stated that he is in that traffic all the time.  The peak is really 3–6 p.m. 
He thinks that 10 pumps are too many. The traffic study needs to be redone.  They need a right turn only 
to get in and out.  This is a small piece of land.  It needs to be smaller, or there will be problems. 
 
Joe Catta, 64 Grove Street, Yalesville, noted that there are already 25 gas stations in the immediate area 
and 3 Dunkin Donuts.  This is a two-lane State road. This would require an exclusive turn lane or traffic 
control.  There are two schools in the area.  He stated that you can’t depend only on the State data.  He
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 9 
 
stated that peak hours are 7am – 9:30am and 4pm – 6:15pm.  He noted that speeds in Wallingford have 
accelerated. 
 
Scott Amore, Jenna Road, stated that he often sees people crossing the street from United Concrete. A 
crosswalk is needed.  He suggested an interconnection with the adjacent property and sidewalks.  This is 
an opportunity to use the conditions of approval to make it safer.  This is a great use of this property. 
 
Ms. Rocha shared her experience at their Naugatuck location with similar traffic concerns, and there 
have been no issues with people making left turns. 
 
Mr. Hipp stated that they did their own sight distance analysis for the driveways, and westbound cars 
can see slowing traffic.  The sight lines exceed the recommended sight distance. He has made note of 
the comments. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo stated that newer data would be helpful. He doesn’t see the use of a Gap 
Analysis. 
 
Commissioner Kohan noted that any business there will have the same issue.  He agreed that this 
business will not create new traffic.  He likes the right-turn-only exit, maybe only for peak hours.  He 
doesn’t think a further traffic study will show any improvements.  
 
Commissioner Seichter stated that he would like to see the traffic study revised. The Commission needs 
to be prudent. 
 
Chairman Fitzsimmons stated that the application will be continued to the November meeting. He asked 
Mr. Pagini to get written comments from the Police Chief. He asked if a right-turn-only exit would work 
and asked the applicant to consider reducing the number of gas pumps. 
 
Hearing no further public comment, Chairman Fitzsimmons called for a motion to continue the public 
hearing. 
 
Commissioner Kohan: Motion to continue the Special Permit request for application #407-26 
for Atlantis Management Group for 124 Church Street to the November meeting. 
 
Commissioner Leonardo: Second 
Vote: Kohan – yes; Leonardo – yes; Seichter – yes; Sanders – yes; Chairman Fitzsimmons  –  
yes. 
The continuation is approved. 
 
4. CT General Statute 8-30g Site Plan / The Metro Realty Management Corp./110 Leigus Road    
#221-26 (continuation)
October 14, 2026 Planning & Zoning Commission Page 10 
 
Commissioner Leonardo noted the additional correspondence.  Letter from Antonio Ulises Ramirez-
Avila, to Wallingford Planning & Zoning Commission received September 21, 2026; letter from Thomas 
Daly, PE, SLR International Corporation to Alison Kapushinski, PE, Town Engineer, dated September 30, 
2026; letter from Tomas Daly, PE, SLR International Corporation to Kevin Pagini, Town Planner, dated 
October 12, 2026; Inspection Report from the Wallingford Fire Marshal received October 14, 2026 and a 
letter from Sebastian Velez, Environmental and Natural Resources Planner regarding the IWWC 
approval. 
 
Atty. Timothy Hollister,  Hinckley, Allen and Snyder in Hartford; Thomas Daly, Civil Engineer, SLR 
Consulting; Kyle Richards, Executive Vice President, Metro Realty; Mark Vertucci, Traffic Engineer with
